'''Carbonic acid''' is a [[chemical compound]] with the chemical formula {{chem2|H2CO3|auto=on}}. The [[molecule]] rapidly converts to [[water]] and [[carbon dioxide]] in the presence of water.<ref name="Loerting2000">{{cite journal |last1=Loerting |first1=Thomas |author1-link=Thomas Loerting The interconversion of carbon dioxide and carbonic acid is related to the [[breathing]] process of all [[aerobic organisms]] and to the [[ocean acidification|acidification of natural waters]].<ref name="Benz2022" />

== History ==
During the early days of chemistry, {{chem2|CO2}} received multiple names. Led by Lavoisier, a group of chemists systematized the nomenclature of chemicals then known. {{chem2|CO2}} was named "carbonic acid" in 1781, because it was produced by combustion of charcoal (''charbon'' in French), and it was considered an acid. Back then, an acid was something that, when dissolved in water, produces red in a litmus test and a distinctive acidic taste. Later, chemists reconceptualized "acid", and no longer accepted {{chem2|CO2}} to be an acid, and "carbonic acid" became the systematic name of {{chem2|H2CO3}} instead. It was thought that {{chem2|H2CO3}} could not exist independently, and could only exist in a solution.<ref name="Lago2024" />

In the 1960s, experimenters produced [[Adduct|adducts]] of {{chem2|H2CO3}}. The [[diethyl ether]] adduct {{chem2|H2CO3*O(CH2CH3)2}} was prepared at -78 °C.<ref name="Galinos1961">{{Cite journal |last=Galinos |first=Andreas G. |last2=Carotti |first2=Arrigo A. |date=February 1961 |title=The Isolation of Etherated Carbonic Acid |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja01464a053 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=83 |issue=3 |pages=752–752 |doi=10.1021/ja01464a053 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The [[dimethyl ether]] adduct {{chem2|H2CO3*O(CH3)2}} was synthesized at -30 °C using dimethyl ether and [[Sodium bicarbonate|sodium carbonate]], and confirmed by chemical, thermochemical, IR, and NMR methods. The pure {{chem2|H2CO3*O(CH3)2}} is a solid that decomposes at 5 °C.<ref name="Gattow1968">{{Cite journal |last=Gattow |first=G. |last2=Gerwarth |first2=U. |date=March 1968 |title=Über chalkogenocarbonate. XXX. Versuche zur Isolierung der „freien kohlensäure”︁ OC(OH) 2 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/zaac.19683570110 |journal=Zeitschrift für anorganische und allgemeine Chemie |language=en |volume=357 |issue=1-2 |pages=78–91 |doi=10.1002/zaac.19683570110 |issn=0044-2313|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1987, gaseous {{chem2|H2CO3}} was prepared by [[thermolysis]] of [[Ammonium bicarbonate|{{Chem2|NH4HCO3}}]], and confirmed by [[Infrared spectroscopy|IR]] and [[collisional activation]] [[mass spectrometry]].<ref name="Terlouw1987">{{Cite journal |last=Terlouw |first=Johan K. |last2=Lebrilla |first2=Carlito B. |last3=Schwarz |first3=Helmut |date=April 1987 |title=Thermolysis of NH 4 HCO 3 —A Simple Route to the Formation of Free Carbonic Acid (H 2 CO 3 ) in the Gas Phase |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anie.198703541 |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English |language=en |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=354–355 |doi=10.1002/anie.198703541 |issn=0570-0833|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 1991, solid {{chem2|H2CO3}} was prepared by solid irradiation of a 1:1 {{Chem2|H2O + CO2}} ice mixture at 20 K.<ref name="Moore1991">{{Cite journal |last=Moore |first=M.H. |last2=Khanna |first2=R.K. |date=January 1991 |title=Infrared and mass spectral studies of proton irradiated H2O + CO2 ice: Evidence for carbonic acid |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0584853991800973 |journal=Spectrochimica Acta Part A: Molecular Spectroscopy |language=en |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=255–262 |doi=10.1016/0584-8539(91)80097-3|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The result of this preparation route is termed {{chem2|α\sH2CO3}}. Another synthesis route was to begin by reacting [[Hydrogen bromide|{{Chem2|HBr}}]] and [[Potassium bicarbonate|{{Chem2|KHCO3}}]] in an aqueous solution, then [[Sublimation (phase transition)|sublimate]] away water at 200 K. Confirmed by [[Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy|FTIR spectroscopy]].<ref name="Lago2024" /> The result of this preparation route is termed {{chem2|β\sH2CO3}}. However, {{chem2|α\sH2CO3}} is later argued to be {{chem2|(CH3)O(COOH)}}, a monomethyl ester.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reisenauer |first=Hans Peter |last2=Wagner |first2=J. Philipp |last3=Schreiner |first3=Peter R. |date=2014-10-27 |title=Gas‐Phase Preparation of Carbonic Acid and Its Monomethyl Ester |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anie.201406969 |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |language=en |volume=53 |issue=44 |pages=11766–11771 |doi=10.1002/anie.201406969 |issn=1433-7851|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

This then leaves the question of why {{chem2|H2CO3}} has "surprising kinetic stability", and why it took so long for solid-state {{chem2|H2CO3}} to be isolated. An explanation using [[transition state theory]] is that pure {{chem2|H2CO3}} is in fact rather [[Metastability|metastable]]. At 300 K, its half-life is theoretically predicted to be ~10<sup>5</sup> years, but the half-life in the presence of 2 water molecules decreases to ~1 minute. In short, water catalyzes the decomposition of {{chem2|H2CO3}}.<ref name="Loerting2000" />

==Anhydrous carbonic acid==
According to quantum chemical calculations, at room temperature (300 K), pure carbonic acid is expected to be a kinetically stable gas.<ref name="Loerting2000" /> There are two main methods to produce [[anhydrous]] carbonic acid: reaction of [[hydrogen chloride]] and [[potassium bicarbonate]] at [[Orders of magnitude (temperature)|100 K]] in [[methanol]] and [[Proton beam|proton irradiation]] of pure [[solid carbon dioxide]].<ref name="Hage1998" /> Chemically, it behaves as a [[diprotic acid|diprotic]] [[Brønsted acid]].<ref name="Pangotra2022" /><ref name="Andersen2002" /><ref name="Winkel2007">{{Cite journal |last1=Winkel |first1=Katrin |last2=Hage |first2=Wolfgang |last3=Loerting |first3=Thomas |last4=Price |first4=Sarah L. |last5=Mayer |first5=Erwin |date=2007-11-01 |title=Carbonic Acid: From Polyamorphism to Polymorphism |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja073594f |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=129 |issue=45 |pages=13863–13871 |doi=10.1021/ja073594f |bibcode=2007JAChS.12913863W |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Carbonic acid [[monomers]] exhibit three [[conformational isomerism|conformational isomers]]: cis–cis, cis–trans, and trans–trans.<ref name="Loerting2010">{{cite journal |author1=Loerting, Thomas |author2=Bernard, Juergen |year=2010 |title=Aqueous Carbonic Acid (H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) |journal=ChemPhysChem |volume=11 |issue=11 |pages=2305–9 |doi=10.1002/cphc.201000220 |pmid=20397242 }}</ref><ref name="Zhao2025">{{Cite journal |last1=Zhao |first1=Yueqi |last2=Tian |first2=Feifei |last3=Sun |first3=Zhaoru |date=2025-05-09 |title=Ab initio deep neural network simulations reveal that carbonic acid dissociation is dominated by minority cis-trans conformers |journal=Science Advances |language=en |volume=11 |issue=19 |article-number=eadu6525 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adu6525 |issn=2375-2548 |pmc=12057677 |pmid=40333980 |bibcode=2025SciA...11.6525Z }}</ref>

At low temperature and [[atmospheric pressure]], solid carbonic acid is [[Amorphous solid|amorphous]] and lacks [[Bragg peak|Bragg peaks]] in [[X-ray diffraction]].<ref name="Winkel2007" /> But at high pressure, carbonic acid crystallizes, and modern analytical spectroscopy can measure its geometry,<ref name="Benz2022" /><ref name="Winkel2007" /> which under certain conditions have [[space group]] [[Cmc21|Cmc2<sub>1</sub>]].<ref name="Spahr2025" />

According to [[neutron diffraction]] of [[deuterium|dideuterated]] carbonic acid ({{chem|D|2|CO|3}}) in a hybrid clamped cell ([[40HNU-VI|Ni–Cr–Al Russian alloy]]/[[Copper beryllium alloy|copper-beryllium]]) at 1.85 GPa, the molecules are planar and form [[Dimerization (chemistry)|dimers]] joined by pairs of [[hydrogen bond]]s. All three [[Carbon–oxygen bond|C-O bonds]] are nearly equidistant at 1.34 [[Angstrom|Å]], intermediate between typical C-O and C=O distances (respectively 1.43 and 1.23 Å). The unusual C-O bond lengths are attributed to delocalized [[Pi bond|π bonding]] in the molecule's center and extraordinarily strong hydrogen bonds. The same effects also induce a very short O—O separation (2.13 Å), through the 136° O-H-O [[angle]] imposed by the doubly hydrogen-bonded 8-membered rings. The crystal has space group [[P21/c|P2<sub>1</sub>/C]].<ref name="Benz2022" /> Longer O—O distances are observed in strong intramolecular hydrogen bonds, e.g. in [[oxalic acid]], where the distances exceed 2.4 Å.<ref name="Winkel2007" /> Trimers and higher polymers are predicted to be even more stable. Based on the stability, it was suggested that solid carbonic acid can be used to [[Carbon sequestration|sequestrate carbon]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tossell |first=J. A. |date=2009-04-01 |title=H 2 CO 3 (s): A New Candidate for CO 2 Capture and Sequestration |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/es802393s |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |language=en |volume=43 |issue=7 |pages=2575–2580 |doi=10.1021/es802393s |issn=0013-936X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Spahr2025" />

==In aqueous solution==
In the presence of even a slight amount of water, carbonic acid [[Dehydration reaction|dehydrates]] to [[carbon dioxide]] and [[water]], which then [[Autocatalysis|catalyzes]] further decomposition.<ref name="Loerting2000" /> 

The [[hydrate|hydration]] [[equilibrium constant]] at 25 °C is {{awrap|[{{chem|H|2|CO|3}}]/[{{CO2}}] ≈ 1.7×10<sup>−3</sup>}} in pure water<ref name="Housecroft2005">{{cite book |last1=Housecroft |first1=C.E. |title=Inorganic Chemistry |last2=Sharpe |first2=A.G. |date=2005 |publisher=Prentice-Pearson-Hall |isbn=0-13-039913-2 |edition=2nd |page=368 |oclc=56834315}}</ref> and ≈ 1.2×10<sup>−3</sup> in [[seawater]].<ref name="Soli2002">{{cite journal |last=Soli |first=A. L. |author2=R. H. Byrne |year=2002 |title=CO<sub>2</sub> system hydration and dehydration kinetics and the equilibrium CO<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> ratio in aqueous NaCl solution |journal=Marine Chemistry |volume=78 |issue=2–3 |pages=65–73 |doi=10.1016/S0304-4203(02)00010-5 |bibcode=2002MarCh..78...65S }}</ref> Hence the majority of carbon dioxide at geophysical or biological [[Surface water|air-water interfaces]] does not convert to carbonic acid, remaining dissolved {{CO2}} gas. However, the [[catalyst|uncatalyzed]] equilibrium is reached quite slowly: the [[rate constant]]s are 0.039 [[Second|s]]<sup>−1</sup> for hydration and 23 s<sup>−1</sup> for dehydration.

===In biological solutions===
In the presence of the enzyme [[carbonic anhydrase]], equilibrium is instead reached rapidly, and the following reaction takes precedence:<ref name="Lindskog_1997">{{cite journal |vauthors=Lindskog S |year=1997 |title=Structure and mechanism of carbonic anhydrase |journal=Pharmacology & Therapeutics |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1016/S0163-7258(96)00198-2 |pmid=9336012}}</ref> <chem display=block>HCO3^- {+} H^+ <=> CO2 {+} H2O</chem>

When the created carbon dioxide exceeds its solubility, gas evolves and a third equilibrium <chem display=block>CO_2 (soln) <=> CO_2 (g)</chem> must also be taken into consideration. The equilibrium constant for this reaction is defined by [[Henry's law#Fundamental types and variants of Henry's law constants|Henry's law]]. 

The two reactions can be combined for the equilibrium in solution: <math chem="" display="block">\begin{align}
\ce{HCO3^{-}{} + H+{} <=> CO2(soln){} + H2O} && K_3 = \frac{[\ce{H+}][\ce{HCO3^-}]}{[\ce{CO2(soln)}]}
\end{align}</math> When Henry's law is used to calculate the denominator '''care is needed''' with regard to units since Henry's law constant can be commonly expressed with 8 different dimensionalities.<ref name="Sander2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Sander |first1=Rolf |last2=Acree |first2=William E. |last3=Visscher |first3=Alex De |last4=Schwartz |first4=Stephen E. |last5=Wallington |first5=Timothy J. |date=2022-01-01 |title=Henry's law constants (IUPAC Recommendations 2021) |journal=Pure and Applied Chemistry |language=en |volume=94 |issue=1 |pages=71–85 |doi=10.1515/pac-2020-0302 |issn=1365-3075|doi-access=free |bibcode=2022PApCh..94...71S }}</ref>

=== In water pH control ===
In wastewater treatment and agriculture irrigation, carbonic acid is used to acidify the water similar to [[sulfuric acid]] and [[sulfurous acid]] produced by sulfur burners.<ref name="Meneses2024">{{Cite web |last=Meneses |first=Adolfo |date=November 19, 2024 |title=Irrigation water acidification using captured CO2; An option to traditional acidification systems. |url=https://www.worldagexpo.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/11/Soil-acidification-r.-1.0.pdf |access-date=November 19, 2024 |website=World Ag Expo}}</ref>

=== Under high CO<sub>2</sub> partial pressure ===
In the [[beverage industry]], sparkling or "fizzy water" is usually referred to as [[carbonated water]]. It is made by dissolving carbon dioxide under a small [[positive pressure]] in water. Many [[soft drink]]s treated the same way [[effervescent|effervesce]].

Significant amounts of molecular {{chem|H|2|CO|3}} exist in aqueous solutions subjected to pressures of multiple [[Gigapascal|gigapascals]] (tens of thousands of atmospheres) in planetary interiors.<ref name="Wang2016">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Hongbo |last2=Zeuschner |first2=Janek |last3=Eremets |first3=Mikhail |last4=Troyan |first4=Ivan |last5=Williams |first5=Jonathon |date=27 January 2016 |title=Stable solid and aqueous H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> from CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O at high pressure and high temperature |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=19902 |bibcode=2016NatSR...619902W |doi=10.1038/srep19902 |pmc=4728613 |pmid=26813580 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Stolte2019">{{cite journal |last1=Stolte |first1=Nore |last2=Pan |first2=Ding |date=4 July 2019 |title=Large presence of carbonic acid in CO<sub>2</sub>-rich aqueous fluids under Earth's mantle conditions |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters |volume=10 |issue=17 |pages=5135–41 |arxiv=1907.01833 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpclett.9b01919 |pmid=31411889 |bibcode=2019JPCL...10.5135S |s2cid=195791860}}</ref> Pressures of 0.6–1.6 [[gigapascal|GPa]] at 100 [[kelvin|K]], and 0.75–1.75 GPa at 300 K are attained in the cores of large icy satellites such as [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]], [[Callisto (moon)|Callisto]], and [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], where water and carbon dioxide are present. Pure carbonic acid, being denser than the ice, is expected to have sunk beneath the ice layers and to separate them from the rocky cores of these moons.<ref name="Saleh2016">{{cite journal |author1=G. Saleh |author2=A. R. Oganov |date=2016 |title=Novel Stable Compounds in the C-H-O Ternary System at High Pressure |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=6 |article-number=32486 |bibcode=2016NatSR...632486S |doi=10.1038/srep32486  |doi-access=free|pmc=5007508 |pmid=27580525}}</ref>

== Relationship to bicarbonate and carbonate ==
[[File:Weak acid speciation.svg|thumb|class=skin-invert-image|right|[[Bjerrum plot]] of speciation for a hypothetical monoprotic acid: AH concentration as a function of the difference between {{Math|''p''K}} and {{Math|''p''H}}]]
Carbonic acid is the formal [[Brønsted–Lowry]] [[conjugate acid]] of the [[bicarbonate]] anion, stable in [[Base (chemistry)|alkaline solution]]. The protonation constants have been measured to great precision, but depend on overall [[ionic strength]] {{Mvar|I}}. The two equilibria most easily measured are as follows: <math chem display="block">\begin{align}
\ce{CO3^{2-}{} + H+{} <=> HCO3^-} && \beta_1 = \frac{[\ce{HCO3^-}]}{[\ce{H+}][\ce{CO3^{2-}}]} \\
\ce{CO3^{2-}{} + 2H+{} <=> H2CO3} && \beta_2 = \frac{[\ce{H2CO3}]}{[\ce{H+}]^2[\ce{CO3^{2-}}]}
\end{align}</math> where brackets indicate the [[concentration]] of [[Species (chemistry)|species]]. At 25 °C, these equilibria empirically satisfy<ref>[[IUPAC]] (2006). "[https://old.iupac.org/publications/scdb/index.html Stability constants]" (database). </ref><math display="block">\begin{alignat}{6}
\log(\beta_1) =&& 0&.54&I^2 - 0&.96&I +&& 9&.93 \\
\log(\beta_2) =&& -2&.5&I^2 - 0&.043&I +&& 16&.07
\end{alignat}</math>{{Math|log(''β''<sub>1</sub>)}} decreases with increasing {{Mvar|I}}, as does {{Math|log(''β''<sub>2</sub>)}}. In a solution absent other ions (e.g. {{Math|''I'' {{=}} 0}}), these curves imply the following [[Dissociation constant|stepwise dissociation constants]]:<math display="block">\begin{alignat}{3}
p\text{K}_1 &= \log(\beta_2) - \log(\beta_1) &= 6.77 \\
p\text{K}_2 &= \log(\beta_1) &= 9.93
\end{alignat}</math> Direct values for these constants in the literature include {{math|''p''K<sub>1</sub> {{=}} 6.35}} and {{math|''p''K<sub>2</sub> - ''p''K<sub>1</sub> {{=}} 3.49}}.<ref name="Pines2016">{{cite journal |last1=Pines |first1=Dina |last2=Ditkovich |first2=Julia |last3=Mukra |first3=Tzach |last4=Miller |first4=Yifat |last5=Kiefer |first5=Philip M. |last6=Daschakraborty |first6=Snehasis |last7=Hynes |first7=James T. |last8=Pines |first8=Ehud |date=2016 |title=How Acidic Is Carbonic Acid? |journal=J Phys Chem B |volume=120 |issue=9 |pages=2440–51 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.5b12428 |pmc=5747581 |pmid=26862781 |bibcode=2016JPCB..120.2440P }}</ref>

To interpret these numbers, note that two chemical species in an acid equilibrium are [[Equinumerosity|equiconcentrated]] when {{Math|''p''K {{=}} ''p''H}}. In particular, the [[extracellular fluid]] ([[cytosol]]) in biological systems exhibits {{Math|''p''H ≈ 7.2}}, so that carbonic acid will be almost 50%-dissociated at equilibrium.

=== Ocean acidification ===
[[File:Carbonate system of seawater.svg|thumb|class=skin-invert-image|upright=1.4|Carbonate speciation in seawater (ionic strength 0.7 mol/dm<sup>3</sup>). The expected change shown is due to the [[Greenhouse gas emissions|current anthropogenic increase]] in [[atmospheric carbon dioxide]] concentration.|left]]

The [[Bjerrum plot]] shows typical equilibrium concentrations, in solution, in [[seawater]], of carbon dioxide and the various species derived from it, as a function of [[pH]].<ref name="Pangotra2022">{{cite journal |last1=Pangotra |first1=Dhananjai |last2=Csepei |first2=Lénárd-István |last3=Roth |first3=Arne |last4=Ponce de León |first4=Carlos |last5=Sieber |first5=Volker |last6=Vieira |first6=Luciana |year=2022 |title=Anodic production of hydrogen peroxide using commercial carbon materials |journal=Applied Catalysis B: Environmental |volume=303 |article-number=120848 |doi=10.1016/j.apcatb.2021.120848 |bibcode=2022AppCB.30320848P |s2cid=240250750}}</ref><ref name="Andersen2002">{{cite journal |last=Andersen |first=C. B. |year=2002 |title=Understanding carbonate equilibria by measuring alkalinity in experimental and natural systems |journal=Journal of Geoscience Education |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=389–403 |doi=10.5408/1089-9995-50.4.389 |bibcode=2002JGeEd..50..389A |s2cid=17094010}}</ref> As human industrialization has [[Greenhouse gas emissions|increased the proportion]] of [[carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere]], the proportion of carbon dioxide dissolved in sea- and freshwater as carbonic acid is also expected to increase. This rise in dissolved acid is also expected to [[Acidifying agent|acidify]] those waters, generating a decrease in pH.<ref name="Caldeira2003">{{cite journal |last=Caldeira |first=K. |author2=Wickett, M. E. |title=Anthropogenic carbon and ocean pH |journal=[[Nature (journal) |Nature]] |volume=425 |issue=6956 |page=365 |year=2003 |s2cid=4417880 |pmid=14508477 |bibcode=2001AGUFMOS11C0385C |doi=10.1038/425365a |doi-access=free |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233227}}</ref><ref name="Sabine2004">{{cite journal |last=Sabine |first=C. L. |year=2004 |title=The Oceanic Sink for Anthropogenic CO<sub>2</sub> |journal=Science |volume=305 |issue=5682 |pages=367–371 |pmid=15256665 |bibcode=2004Sci...305..367S |hdl=10261/52596 |hdl-access=free |s2cid=5607281 |doi=10.1126/science.1097403 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1097403 |access-date=22 June 2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080706143710/http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/short/305/5682/367 |archive-date=6 July 2008|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It has been estimated that the increase in dissolved carbon dioxide has already caused the ocean's average surface pH to decrease by about 0.1 from historical pre-industrial levels.
